analogy.p: Think of a sustainable city as a household that lives within its budget. A household that spends more each month than it earns (using more water, energy and land than nature can replace) eventually runs out of savings and leaves debts for its children. Insulating, recycling and cutting car use are like cutting bills, reusing items, and planting a vegetable patch so the family stays healthy and never overspends. The analogy breaks down because a city has millions of people with conflicting interests who cannot simply agree a family budget, and because environmental 'debts' such as climate change affect people far away and far into the future.
analogy.t: A city as a household with a budget

bullets: **Sustainable urban living** = a way of living in a city that meets the needs of people today **without damaging the ability of future generations to meet their needs**.
The spec names three features: **water and energy conservation**, **waste recycling**, and **creating green space**.
It also names **reducing traffic congestion** through urban transport strategies, with a located example.
Typical command words: **Describe** (say what), **Explain** (say how or why, using 'because'), **Assess/Evaluate** (weigh good and bad and reach a judgement).
Typical mark allocations: 1-2 mark definitions, 4 mark 'explain how', and 6 or 9 mark 'evaluate' or 'to what extent' questions.

Examples you can use: a UK city such as Bristol (MetroBus, cycle routes, Clean Air Zone, European Green Capital 2015), plus BedZED in London, Freiburg's Vauban district in Germany and Curitiba's bus system in Brazil.
This sits inside the wider urban unit: urban growth, urban change in a UK city, and urban sustainability.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8035 (Paper 2, Urban issues and challenges) asks you to know the **features of sustainable urban living**: **water and energy conservation**, **waste recycling** and **creating green space**. You must also know how **urban transport strategies** are used to **reduce traffic congestion**, and be able to give a named example of how this is done in a city. Questions normally ask you to describe, explain or evaluate, so you need the idea, the reason it works and its limitations. Sustainable urban living is the 'solutions' end of the topic: after learning about the problems of rapid urban growth, you now learn how cities try to fix them.

bullets: **Environmental sustainability**: protecting the natural world, using resources carefully, cutting pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
**Social sustainability**: fairness, good health, decent homes, access to services, and a strong community for everyone, including poorer groups.
**Economic sustainability**: jobs and growth that can continue over time, and schemes that are affordable to run for many years.
**Ecological footprint** = the area of land and sea needed to supply a person's or city's resources and absorb their waste. A sustainable city aims to shrink this.
Sustainability is about the **long term**: a scheme that helps now but harms future generations is not sustainable.
Trade-offs are common. For example, a congestion charge helps the environment but may hurt low-income drivers (social) and shops (economic).
The word 'sustainable' on its own earns no marks; you must say **what is sustained, for whom and why**.
core.p: The usual definition is **development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**. For a city this means living in a way that does not use up resources or damage the environment faster than they can be replaced, while still keeping people healthy, employed and happy. Geographers describe three linked parts, called the **three pillars of sustainability**: **environmental**, **social** and **economic**. A strategy is only truly sustainable if it works across all three, so a scheme that cuts pollution but is unaffordable for ordinary people is not fully sustainable.

bullets: **Resource demand**: large populations need constant supplies of water, electricity, gas and food, often brought in from far away.
**Waste**: cities produce large volumes of household, commercial and construction waste; if landfilled it uses land and releases **methane**, a greenhouse gas.
**Air pollution**: traffic and industry release nitrogen dioxide and particulates, harming health (asthma, heart and lung disease).
**Urban heat island effect**: dark surfaces such as tarmac and roofs absorb heat and buildings trap it, so city centres are warmer than the countryside.
**Surface runoff**: concrete and tarmac are impermeable, so rain runs quickly into drains and can cause **flash flooding**.
**Urban sprawl** swallows farmland and greenfield land and increases the distance people travel.
**Inequality**: poorer residents may live in the worst housing and the most polluted areas, a social sustainability problem.
Sustainable living features are designed to reduce each of these problems.
core.h: Why cities struggle to be sustainable
core.p: Cities concentrate huge numbers of people in a small area, so they take in vast amounts of water, food, energy and materials and produce huge amounts of waste, heat and pollution. Most of the world's energy use and greenhouse gas emissions come from urban areas. Cities also cover natural land with concrete and tarmac, which changes the local environment. Understanding these problems helps you explain why each sustainable feature is needed.

bullets: **Rainwater harvesting**: collecting rain from roofs in butts or tanks to water gardens or flush toilets, reducing demand on mains water.
**Greywater recycling**: reusing lightly used water from sinks, showers and baths for flushing toilets or irrigation.
**Water-saving appliances**: dual-flush toilets, low-flow showerheads, aerated taps and efficient washing machines cut use per person.
**Water meters** charge by use, giving households a financial reason to save water.
**Fixing leaks**: ageing city pipes lose a large share of treated water, so repairing them saves large amounts.
**Sustainable drainage systems (SuDS)**, such as permeable paving, swales and ponds, let water soak away slowly, reducing flood risk and recharging groundwater.
**Public education** campaigns and hosepipe bans during droughts reduce demand.
Why it works: less water abstracted means rivers and wetlands keep healthy flows, and less energy is used for treatment and pumping.
Limitation: harvesting and greywater systems cost money to install, so uptake can be low unless grants or building regulations require them.
core.p: **Water conservation** means using water more carefully so that less is taken from rivers, reservoirs and aquifers and less has to be treated and pumped. This matters because many cities, especially in drier or fast-growing regions, face water stress. In the UK, the south-east has relatively low rainfall but a high population, so demand can approach supply in dry summers. Conserving water also saves the energy used for pumping and treating it, which links water and energy sustainability.

bullets: **Insulation**: loft, cavity wall and floor insulation cut heat loss so less fuel is burned to heat homes.
**Double or triple glazing** and draught-proofing reduce heat escaping through windows and gaps.
**Energy-efficient appliances and LED lighting** use far less electricity; energy labels help consumers choose.
**Smart meters** show real-time use, which encourages people to cut waste.
**Solar panels** (photovoltaic) on roofs generate electricity; **solar water heating** reduces gas or electricity use.
**Passive solar design**: south-facing windows capture low winter sun, with thick insulation and thermal mass to hold heat.
**Combined heat and power (CHP)** and district heating use waste heat to warm many buildings.
**Green roofs and trees** insulate buildings and shade them in summer, cutting cooling needs.
Building regulations and **Energy Performance Certificates** push builders and landlords to improve efficiency.
Limitation: renewable technology and retrofitting have high upfront costs; many tenants cannot make changes themselves.
core.p: **Energy conservation** means using less energy for the same result, through better design and behaviour, while **renewable energy** replaces fossil fuels with sources that are naturally replenished. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which increases the enhanced greenhouse effect and causes climate change. Cities use energy for heating, lighting, appliances and transport, so cutting demand and switching to cleaner supply is central to sustainable living. Insulation and efficient design are usually the cheapest and most effective first steps.

bullets: **Kerbside collections** of separated paper, glass, metal, plastic and food waste make recycling easy and raise recycling rates.
**Recycling centres** and bring banks allow bulky or hard-to-recycle items to be processed.
**Food waste composting or anaerobic digestion** turns scraps into compost and biogas (a fuel), instead of producing methane in landfill.
**Reduce**: less packaging, refill shops and bag charges stop waste being created in the first place.
**Reuse**: charity shops, repair cafes and online resale give products a second life.

**Why recycle?** It saves raw materials (for example bauxite for aluminium), uses less energy (recycling aluminium uses only a small fraction of the energy of making it from ore), cuts landfill and lowers emissions.
**Energy from waste**: incineration that generates electricity is better than landfill but releases CO2 and needs filtering.
Problems: collection and sorting cost money, contamination spoils loads, some plastics are hard to recycle, and people may not take part.
Incentives and laws, such as landfill tax and recycling targets, make recycling more attractive than dumping.
core.h: Waste recycling and the waste hierarchy
core.p: Sustainable cities try to produce less waste and to treat the waste they do produce as a resource rather than rubbish. The **waste hierarchy** ranks options from most to least sustainable: **reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, dispose**. **Recycling** means processing used materials such as paper, glass, metals, plastics and food waste into new products. It cuts the need for virgin raw materials, saves energy and reduces landfill, which is why it is a named feature in the specification.

bullets: **Environmental benefits**: absorbs CO2, filters dust and pollutants, reduces the **urban heat island effect** and provides habitat for birds, insects and mammals.
**Flood reduction**: soil and plants intercept rain and slow runoff, lowering the risk of flash floods.
**Social benefits**: places to exercise, play and meet; linked to lower stress and better mental health; community gardens build neighbourhood links.
**Economic benefits**: attractive areas raise property values and attract visitors and businesses; allotments and urban farms supply local food.
**Green roofs and walls** add planting where land is scarce and insulate buildings.
**Brownfield redevelopment** can turn derelict land into parks, while **green belts** limit sprawl around cities.
**Urban greening policies** include tree planting, protected local nature reserves and making new developments include open space.
Limitation: land in cities is expensive and competes with housing; parks need long-term money for maintenance, and not all areas have equal access.
core.p: **Green space** means parks, gardens, playing fields, allotments, trees, green roofs and wildlife corridors in towns and cities. The spec lists 'creating green space' because it improves the urban environment in several ways at once. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and some pollutants, provide shade and release water vapour that cools the air, while open land lets rainwater soak in. Green space also benefits people's physical and mental health and provides habitats for wildlife, so it supports all three pillars of sustainability.

bullets: **Causes**: high car ownership, rush-hour commuting, rapid growth of population, urban sprawl that increases travel distance, narrow historic road layouts and poor public transport.
**Environmental impacts**: more exhaust fumes (nitrogen dioxide, particulates, CO2), noise, and stop-start driving that burns more fuel.
**Health impacts**: air pollution is linked to asthma and heart and lung disease; stress and less exercise from car use.
**Economic impacts**: lost working time, delayed deliveries and higher business costs.
**Social impacts**: noise, road danger and severed communities; people without cars are disadvantaged if buses are caught in traffic.
Building more roads often draws in even more traffic (induced demand), so the problem returns: this is why cities prefer **demand management** to simply adding capacity.
Solution aim: make alternatives to the private car **cheaper, quicker and more attractive**.
core.p: **Traffic congestion** occurs when the number of vehicles exceeds the capacity of the road network, so journeys slow down and queues form. Most UK city roads were laid out long before cars became common, so they are often narrow and cannot be widened without demolishing buildings. High car ownership, commuting into centres at the same time each day (rush hour), and dependence on cars for school and shopping runs all add to the problem. Congestion is a key target of sustainable urban transport policy because its effects are environmental, social and economic.

bullets: **Public transport improvements**: more frequent, cheaper and faster buses, trams and trains, with integrated tickets and real-time information.
**Bus lanes and priority signals** let buses bypass queues so they become faster than cars.
**Park and ride**: car parks on the edge of the city linked to the centre by frequent buses, so drivers avoid entering the centre.
**Congestion charging and low-emission zones** make drivers (often of older, polluting vehicles) pay to enter central areas, which reduces traffic and funds public transport.
**Cycle lanes, cycle hire and safe routes** (and pedestrianised streets) encourage walking and cycling, which have no emissions and improve health.
**Car sharing and car clubs**, with priority lanes or parking, reduce the number of cars per person.
**Parking controls**: limiting and pricing city-centre spaces discourages commuter driving.
**Traffic calming and one-way systems** manage flow and make streets safer.
**Electric vehicles** and charging points reduce emissions, though they do not cut congestion on their own.
**Planning**: mixed-use developments and homes near jobs reduce the need to travel.
core.h: Urban transport strategies to reduce congestion
core.p: Cities use a package of **traffic management strategies** that either encourage people to leave the car at home (the 'carrot') or make driving into the centre less attractive (the 'stick'). Successful schemes usually combine both, because improving buses alone will not change behaviour unless driving is also made harder or costlier. You should be able to describe several strategies and the reasoning behind each one.

bullets: **Park and ride**: reduces central traffic and pollution and is cheap to use, but needs land on the edge of the city and some people still prefer to drive in.
**Bus lanes**: cheap and quick to install and speed up buses, but take road space from cars and can increase congestion on other lanes.
**Congestion charge**: strong deterrent that raises money for public transport, but it can hit low-income drivers and businesses hardest and is unpopular.
**Low-emission or clean air zones**: improve air quality and encourage cleaner vehicles, but owners of older vehicles face costs or must replace them.
**Cycling infrastructure**: healthy, cheap and zero-emission, but only suits shorter trips, weather matters, and safety worries stop many people.
**Public transport**: low carbon per passenger and reduces car use, but needs large long-term investment and must be reliable.
**Electric vehicles**: cut tailpipe emissions but still use road space, and their electricity and batteries have environmental costs.
Judgement tip: say that **no single strategy is enough**, and that the best results come from combining attractive alternatives with measures that discourage driving.
core.h: Evaluating transport strategies: advantages and problems
core.p: For high-mark answers you must weigh strategies, not just list them. Each has strengths and weaknesses depending on the city, cost and public attitude. A strong evaluation says who benefits, who loses and whether the effect is likely to last. Reaching a supported judgement, such as 'a combination of strategies is most effective', is what moves an answer into the top level.

bullets: **Bristol public transport**: the **MetroBus** bus rapid transit routes use dedicated lanes and guided busways to link suburbs with the centre, aiming to give faster journeys than car travel.
**Bristol park and ride** sites on the edge of the city link to the centre by bus.
**Bristol Clean Air Zone** (introduced in November 2022) charges the most polluting vehicles to enter the central area, aiming to cut nitrogen dioxide.
**Bristol cycling**: cycle lanes, shared bike schemes and the Bristol and Bath Railway Path make cycling a realistic commuting option; Bristol was **European Green Capital in 2015**.
**Curitiba, Brazil**: a pioneering **bus rapid transit** system with dedicated lanes and raised tube stations; high public transport use keeps congestion low for a city of its size.
**Freiburg (Vauban), Germany**: car-free streets, a tram link and extensive cycling make low car ownership normal.
**Method for exam answers**: name the scheme, state what it does, give a figure or fact if known, then explain how it reduces congestion and one limitation.
Include a **named example** in every 'using an example' question, as unlabelled general points cannot access the top marks.
core.h: Example: how a city reduces congestion (Bristol, plus world examples)
core.p: AQA expects an example of how urban transport strategies are used to reduce traffic congestion, so use one you can recall in detail from your lessons. Bristol is a common UK example. It is the largest city in the South West and has serious congestion because of high car ownership and a historic road layout around the River Avon. Check the exact names, dates and figures against your own class notes, and only include details you are confident about.

bullets: **Compact city / mixed use**: homes, shops, jobs and services close together so people can walk or cycle and cut car trips.
**Eco-homes**: high insulation, efficient heating, solar panels, rainwater harvesting and sustainably sourced materials.
**Brownfield first**: reusing derelict land protects green belts and countryside.
**Affordable and mixed housing** supports social sustainability by keeping communities mixed and avoiding segregation.
**Local jobs and food**: community enterprises, allotments and farmers' markets keep money and resources local.
**Community involvement** (residents helping plan schemes) makes them more likely to be accepted and maintained.
Limitation: sustainable housing can cost more to build, and 'eco' homes may be unaffordable for those who need them most.
Link: these ideas also appear in urban regeneration and in the 'sustainable urban living' parts of case studies of UK cities.
core.h: Sustainable design: housing and whole communities
core.p: Sustainable living does not only depend on individual features; whole neighbourhoods can be designed to be sustainable. **BedZED** (Beddington Zero Energy Development) in Sutton, south London, is a well-known example of a low-carbon housing community with highly insulated homes, south-facing windows, solar panels, water saving and good links to public transport. The Vauban district of Freiburg combines energy-efficient housing, green space, low car use and a strong community. Compact, mixed-use design reduces how far people need to travel.

bullets: **Environmental versus economic**: a congestion charge cuts pollution but may discourage shoppers and businesses from the centre.
**Social versus economic**: eco-housing may be costly, so affordable homes might be sacrificed or built to lower standards.
**Short term versus long term**: insulation or solar panels cost more now but save money and carbon later.
**Who pays?** Taxpayers, developers or drivers; the answer affects whether a scheme is seen as fair.
**Who benefits?** Cyclists and residents of central areas may gain while outer commuters with poor bus links lose.
**Success depends on people**: schemes fail if people do not change behaviour, so incentives, education and consultation matter.
**Government role**: national targets, funding, building regulations and local planning shape what is built.
A good evaluative judgement uses phrases such as 'overall...', 'the most effective is...because...', and 'this depends on...'.
core.h: Balancing the three pillars: trade-offs and planning
core.p: Real urban decisions rarely score well on all three pillars of sustainability at once, so planners must weigh costs and benefits. For example, a park and ride scheme may help the environment and economy but use up green belt land on the edge of the city. Local councils, businesses, residents and the government all have different priorities, so decisions involve compromise. In longer answers, showing awareness of these trade-offs is a mark of top-level thinking.

bullets: **Urban change in a UK city**: regeneration schemes often include green space, cycling and sustainable housing.
**Climate change**: reducing energy use and car travel lowers greenhouse gas emissions, tackling the enhanced greenhouse effect.
**Resource management**: water and energy conservation tie into the water and energy resource units.
**Hazards**: SuDS and green space reduce flood risk, which links to river flooding and urban hydrology.
**Development**: in LICs and NEEs, informal settlements need sustainable water, sanitation and waste solutions.
**Data skills**: be ready to interpret graphs of recycling rates, air pollution levels, traffic counts or maps showing green space.
**Fieldwork/decision making**: you may be asked to recommend which strategy is best and justify it with evidence.
Always finish a 6 or 9 mark answer with a **judgement** that answers the exact question asked.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam-linked skills
core.p: This spec point connects with several other parts of the course, and examiners reward linking ideas together. Sustainable urban living responds to the problems that come from rapid urbanisation, such as pollution, waste and congestion, and it contributes to wider global aims such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions. You may also meet it in fieldwork-style or decision-making questions in Paper 3, where you weigh evidence about a proposed scheme.

exam: **Command words**: 'Describe' = what it is or does; 'Explain' = how/why with linked reasons; 'Assess' or 'Evaluate' = weigh advantages and disadvantages and reach a judgement.
**1-2 mark questions**: give a precise definition or a single feature, such as 'recycling turns waste into new products, reducing landfill'.
**4 mark 'explain how' questions**: aim for two developed points, each with a feature, a link word ('so', 'because', 'which means') and a result for people or the environment.
**6 mark questions** (levels): use a named example, at least two strategies, a balance of advantages and disadvantages and a final judgement.
**Model chain of reasoning**: strategy -> action -> effect -> impact on sustainability (for example, bus lanes -> faster buses -> more people leave cars -> less congestion and pollution).
**Always link to a pillar**: say whether a point is environmental, social or economic; examiners reward balanced coverage.
**Use data**: when given graphs or tables (recycling rates, air quality, traffic counts), quote figures, describe the trend and then explain it.
**Name the example** for 'using an example' questions: place, scheme name, what it does and one fact.
**Evaluation phrases**: 'however', 'this depends on', 'the most effective because', 'in the long term', 'for low-income residents'.
**Do not write** vague words like 'good', 'bad' or 'eco-friendly' without saying why.
**Time check**: roughly one mark per minute; spend longest on the highest tariff questions.

mistakes.r: Sustainable means meeting present needs without harming future generations, and it covers environmental, social and economic aspects.
Reusing means using an item again as it is; recycling means breaking the material down to make new products.
mistakes.w: 'Recycling and reusing are the same thing.'

mistakes.r: It reduces the number of cars entering the centre; it does not remove all traffic, and some people still drive in.
mistakes.w: 'Park and ride gets rid of all cars in the city.'

mistakes.r: It discourages some journeys and raises funds, but congestion is reduced rather than removed, and it can disadvantage low-income drivers.
It absorbs CO2 and pollutants, cools the air, reduces flooding, supports wildlife and improves health.
mistakes.w: 'Green space just makes cities look nice.'

mistakes.r: Write a developed point: strategy, what it does, why it reduces congestion or pollution (use 'because').
Use a named place with specific details and finish with a clear, justified judgement.
mistakes.w: Answering a 6 mark question with no named example or judgement.

mistakes.r: They produce clean electricity in use but have costs and impacts from manufacture and installation.
More road space can generate extra traffic; demand management and alternatives to cars are usually more sustainable.

summary: The specification asks you to know the features of sustainable urban living (water and energy conservation, waste recycling and creating green space) and how urban transport strategies reduce traffic congestion, with a located example. It matters because sustainable cities cut pollution and resource use while keeping people healthy, and it appears in Paper 2 as describe, explain and evaluate questions.

terms.d: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

Living in cities in ways that reduce resource use and environmental damage while keeping people healthy and communities fair, for example by conserving water and energy, recycling waste and creating green space.
The area of land and sea needed to provide the resources a person, city or country uses and to absorb the waste it produces.
Using water more efficiently and reducing waste so that less is abstracted from the environment, for example by rainwater harvesting and water-saving devices.
Reducing energy use by improving efficiency and changing behaviour, for example through insulation, LED lighting and efficient appliances.
Energy from sources that are naturally replenished, such as solar, wind, hydroelectric and tidal power.
Processing used materials into new products so that fewer raw materials are used and less waste goes to landfill.
A ranking of waste management options from most to least sustainable: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, dispose.
Areas of vegetation in towns and cities such as parks, gardens, trees, allotments and green roofs.
The effect where a city is warmer than the surrounding countryside because buildings and tarmac absorb and trap heat.
A situation where the number of vehicles exceeds road capacity, causing slow, queuing traffic.
A scheme where car parks on the edge of a city are linked to the centre by frequent public transport, so drivers leave their cars outside.
A fee paid by drivers to enter a defined area of a city, used to reduce traffic and raise money for transport.
Features such as permeable paving, ponds and swales that let rainwater soak away slowly and reduce surface runoff and flooding.
Land that has been previously built on and is now derelict or unused, available for redevelopment.
A bus system with dedicated lanes and priority at junctions that gives fast, reliable journeys similar to a tram.

worked.ans: Rainwater harvesting and water-saving appliances reduce the amount of water that has to be taken from rivers and reservoirs (1), which protects water supplies for future generations and saves the energy used to treat and pump water (1). Insulating homes and fitting solar panels reduces the amount of fossil fuel burned for heating and electricity (1), which lowers CO2 emissions and reduces the enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change (1).
worked.q: Explain how water and energy conservation can make a city more sustainable. (4 marks)
steps: Plan two developed points: one on water, one on energy.
Use 'because' or 'so' to link each idea.

worked.ans: (a) 72 000 more tonnes recycled (2). (b) 54% of waste is not recycled (1). Check: 54% of 400 000 = 216 000 tonnes, and 184 000 + 216 000 = 400 000.
worked.q: A city produced 400 000 tonnes of household waste in a year. Its recycling rate rose from 28% to 46% over five years, assuming waste produced stayed the same. (a) Calculate how many more tonnes were recycled. (b) State the percentage of waste not recycled at 46%. (3 marks)

worked.ans: Congestion charging is effective because it makes driving into the centre more expensive, so fewer people drive and traffic and air pollution fall; for example, Bristol's Clean Air Zone charges the most polluting vehicles to enter the centre, which encourages drivers to switch to cleaner vehicles or other transport (2). The money raised can be spent on buses and cycle routes, which gives people alternatives (1). However, charges can hit low-income drivers and local businesses hardest and are often unpopular, so they only work if alternatives are available (2). Other strategies such as park and ride, bus lanes and cycle lanes help people change habit without a penalty, though they take up road space or land (1). Overall, congestion charging is effective but not the single most effective measure; it works best as part of a package with strong public transport, because people will only leave their cars if there is a convenient alternative (1).
worked.q: 'Congestion charging is the most effective way of reducing traffic in cities.' To what extent do you agree? Use an example. (6 marks)
steps: Strengths of charging: deters drivers, reduces pollution, raises money for buses.
Weaknesses: unfair to low-income drivers, may harm businesses, unpopular.
Compare with other strategies: park and ride, bus lanes, cycling.
